facts.claim: Noah Kahan wrote 'She Calls Me Back' alone, and both the solo and duet versions credit him as the only songwriter.
The song was produced by Kahan together with Gabe Simon, who co-produced the whole Stick Season album.
Songfacts says Gabe Simon played all the instruments on the track (percussion, drums, organ, bass, and electric, baritone and acoustic guitars), with Kahan also on guitar.
Stick Season was recorded at Guilford Sound in Guilford, Vermont, and The Study in Nashville.

The Musgraves duet was released October 6, 2023, as a reworked version of a song from Stick Season. It adds a new second verse sung by Musgraves from the partner's perspective, and the two sing the final chorus together.

Kahan told Rolling Stone that after finishing the album he wondered about hearing Kacey Musgraves on several songs. He said getting her on this one was as simple as asking, and that she picked this song herself.
Musgraves recorded her part while Kahan was on tour. He said her verse lets the song move toward resolve instead of the bitter tension of the original.
Kahan and Musgraves first performed the song together live at Nashville's Ryman Auditorium during Musgraves' Deeper Well release show, about six months after the duet came out.
The duet followed Kahan's other 2023 collaborations 'Dial Drunk' with Post Malone and 'Call Your Mom' with Lizzy McAlpine.
Kahan, a Vermont native, signed with Republic Records in 2017. Stick Season (2022) was his commercial breakthrough after earlier cult-favorite albums.

research.lineage: The song sits in the folk-pop and indie-folk singer-songwriter tradition, with Americana and country crossover through Musgraves and faint touches of 1980s heartland rock and power pop.

draft:
"This town's the same as you left it, your page was blank, but I read it." That line holds the whole problem of **She Calls Me Back (with Kacey Musgraves)**. One person left. One stayed. The one who stayed is still reading meaning into silence, still dialing a number from memory, still treating a callback as the only proof that everything's alright. Noah Kahan wrote the song alone, and it sounds like a private ledger. The repeated chorus sets heaven in someone's eyes against a narrator who "was not baptized," someone close to grace but never let in.

What makes the original sting is how clearly the narrator sees the obsession and can't stop it. "Why am I so obsessive?" isn't rhetorical. It sits in a rush of questions, one sentence tumbling into the next, the way thoughts go at 2 a.m. The verses swing between self-sacrifice and self-pity: he could be her sacrifice, an old tattoo, someone who lives "to die while saving you." It's grand and a little ridiculous, and the song knows it. The pain is real, and so is the self-justification. Neither cancels the other.

Then comes the confession that reframes everything: "I was too afraid of livin' life in your footsteps." He didn't follow. That fits *Stick Season*, Kahan's breakthrough album and a record about staying put in small-town Vermont, cut between Guilford Sound in Vermont and The Study in Nashville. Much of his writing comes from the person who didn't leave, and here he admits that staying was fear, not loyalty.

The duet changes the angle. Musgraves chose this song herself when Kahan asked, and she sings a new second verse from the partner's side. She answers the restless questions in kind, with no sleep, every song in a minor key, and the other person showing up in every dream. Then she offers promises about oceans drying and rivers freezing. Kahan said her verse moves the song toward resolve and away from the bitter tension of the solo version. Both voices take the last chorus together, and the one-sided call becomes a two-way line.

The sound stays plain and urgent. A strummed acoustic guitar drives it at a moderate clip, over a simple bass line and steady drums with a snare that pushes hard. Gabe Simon, Kahan's co-producer, played nearly everything, and the room feels natural and clean. Kahan's voice is raw and earnest, and Musgraves' harmony sits close against it and smooths the edges. It's folk-pop with a faint heartland-rock spine, built to be shouted in a car.

The song lets you feel both ends of a stalled phone line at once: the shame of still dialing, and the quiet relief of finding out the other person never stopped either.
